timing_advance_vs_rpm_iat:
Thermal-compensation surface for ignition. Cold dense charge lets the ECU advance more; hot charge gets retarded to keep knock margin. The surface learns the ECU's actual (RPM, IAT) → timing map, so we read deviations from what the engine *normally* does at this thermal+rpm operating point — ambient-invariant by construction (the same IAT bin sees summer afternoons and winter mornings).

Catches:
* Sustained knock-retard activity (negative residuals   clustered at the hot-IAT side of the surface — detonation   triggers spark pull-back).
* Thermal-compensation or knock-control drift. A biased IAT   that the ECU itself uses for timing is a common-mode fault   and is not identifiable from this surface alone.
* Firmware / calibration drift after an ECU re-flash.

Complementary to ``timing_advance_vs_rpm_load`` (load-axis compensation) — both feed the same timing output through different physical axes.
